x-m-el-sta-01.title: Can we trust that survey result?
x-m-el-sta-01.goal: Pick out the information you need to check before accepting a sample survey result as a statement about everyone, and rewrite a sentence to fit the range that was actually surveyed.
x-m-el-sta-01.material: An article appeared in the school newspaper. Title: '72% of all 600 students are satisfied with school lunch!' Small print under the article: 'Survey summary: 100 questionnaires were collected, and 72 of them were marked "satisfied."' The article does not say who the questionnaires were handed out to or how, or what sentence was used to ask the question.
x-m-el-sta-01.thinking.0: Sort out the information you need and don't need to trust a result
x-m-el-sta-01.thinking.1: Notice the difference between who was surveyed and who the claim is about
x-m-el-sta-01.thinking.2: Narrow a claim so it fits the evidence
x-m-el-sta-01.prereq.0: The meaning of a sample survey and a full survey (census)
x-m-el-sta-01.prereq.1: Writing a ratio as a percentage
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.prompt: To decide whether this article can be trusted, choose everything you must ask the school newspaper club.
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.hint.0: Put the group the article talks about (all 600 students) next to the people who actually answered (100 questionnaires) and compare them.
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine how the result would differ for the same 100 questionnaires if they were handed out in front of the lunchroom versus drawn from a name list.
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.o.a: Which students the 100 questionnaires were given to, and in what way
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.r.a: You pointed out that the way the sample was chosen can tilt the result to one side.
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.o.b: Whether the satisfaction rate in the same survey last year was also around 70%
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.r.b: Even if last year's value is similar, that does not confirm that the 100 questionnaires collected this time represent all students.
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.o.c: Whether the question is neutral, like 'Are you satisfied?', or whether it nudges people toward one answer
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.r.c: You considered that the wording of a question can move the answers.
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.o.d: The share of questionnaires returned out of those handed out, and what kind of students did not turn one in
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.r.d: You considered that the students who did not respond may have different opinions from the result.
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.o.e: Whether 72 divided by 100 really gives the 72% shown in the article
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.r.e: The calculation is correct. But a correct calculation is a separate matter from the sample representing all students.
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.explain: The result can be tilted depending on who was asked, what sentence was used, and who did not respond. Comparing with last year's value or checking a simple ratio calculation does not tell you whether this sample is representative.
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.acc.0: You pointed out sample selection and non-response. Checking the question wording as well would make it more complete.
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s1.acc.1: You pointed out sample selection and question wording. Checking who the non-responding students are as well would make it more complete.
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s2.prompt: Using only what you know now, honestly rewrite the article's title sentence. (Make clear what group the percentage is about.)
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s2.hint.0: Write the denominator clearly, like '72 out of 100,' not just 'of 72.'
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s2.hint.1: Add words that narrow the group, such as 'who answered.'
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: In your sentence, is it clear whether the 72% refers to '100 students' or '600 students'?
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Could a newspaper reader read this sentence and mistake it for the opinion of all students?
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s2.model.0: Of the 100 students who returned the questionnaire, 72 said they were satisfied with school lunch.
x-m-el-sta-01.s.s2.model.1: 72% of the 100 students who responded to the survey were satisfied, but it is hard to say that this is the opinion of all students.

x-m-el-sta-02.title: The flaw in the report 'Forty students is enough'
x-m-el-sta-02.goal: Notice that even a large sample is hard to trust if the way it was chosen is biased, and fix how the sample is chosen.
x-m-el-sta-02.material: Sujin wrote the report below to find out 'How much video do students at our school watch each day?' There are 600 students in the school.
x-m-el-sta-02.thinking.0: Find the error in the report's reasoning
x-m-el-sta-02.thinking.1: Tell apart the roles of sample size and sample selection method
x-m-el-sta-02.thinking.2: Suggest a better way to choose a sample
x-m-el-sta-02.prereq.0: The meaning of population and sample
x-m-el-sta-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line that makes Sujin's conclusion hard to trust.
x-m-el-sta-02.s.s1.hint.0: Tell apart whom each line is about, how many, and what it is based on.
x-m-el-sta-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether students who come to borrow books and students who don't might differ in how much video they watch.
x-m-el-sta-02.s.s1.line.0: At the library entrance, 40 students who came to borrow books were asked how long they watch video each day.
x-m-el-sta-02.s.s1.line.1: The 40 students' average daily viewing time was 1.5 hours.
x-m-el-sta-02.s.s1.line.2: Forty is a large enough number, so this result can be trusted.
x-m-el-sta-02.s.s1.line.3: So we estimate that the average daily video viewing time of all students at our school is also about 1.5 hours.
x-m-el-sta-02.s.s1.explain: Line 1 gathers only students who came to borrow books, so the result may lean toward shorter viewing times. Line 3 says a large number can be trusted, but a sample chosen in a biased way keeps its bias even if you add more people. Line 4 applies that sample's result directly to all students. For line 2 (the calculation result), this report alone gives no grounds to object.
x-m-el-sta-02.s.s2.prompt: How could Sujin change the survey method so the conclusion is more trustworthy? Write what to change and why.
x-m-el-sta-02.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether you could use a list the school already has, such as by grade and class.
x-m-el-sta-02.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. From the student name list, ...
x-m-el-sta-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does the method you wrote give every student a similar chance of being chosen?
x-m-el-sta-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write only 'use more people'?
x-m-el-sta-02.s.s2.model.0: Don't ask only students who come to borrow books. Pick 40 students by drawing numbers at random from the list of all students. Students who come to the library may lean toward watching less video.
x-m-el-sta-02.s.s2.model.1: Pick students evenly, in the same proportion from each grade and class. Then the sample represents all students.

x-m-el-sta-03.title: Two classes with the same mean: really similar?
x-m-el-sta-03.goal: Know that distributions can differ even when the means are equal, choose the information needed for comparison, and make such an example yourself.
x-m-el-sta-03.material: Class 1 and Class 2 of grade 2 each have 5 students, and both have a math test mean of 70 points. Seungho said, 'Since the means are the same, the score distributions of the two classes must be similar too.'
x-m-el-sta-03.thinking.0: Choose the information needed to check a claim
x-m-el-sta-03.thinking.1: Make an example where the mean and the median differ
x-m-el-sta-03.thinking.2: Explain the misunderstanding that comes from stating only the mean
x-m-el-sta-03.prereq.0: The meaning of mean (arithmetic mean) and median
x-m-el-sta-03.prereq.1: Arranging numbers in order of size
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.prompt: What information do you need to check whether Seungho is right? Choose everything that is needed.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.hint.0: Think of two or more sets of 5 scores with a mean of 70, and compare how different they can be from each other.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.hint.1: Make a list of what you cannot know from the mean alone.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.o.a: How many questions were on the test the two classes took
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.r.a: You are comparing scores from the same test, so the number of questions gives no new information for comparing distributions.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.o.b: The highest score and the lowest score in each class
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.r.b: You chose information that shows how spread out the scores are.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.o.c: Whether each class's mean is exactly the same to the first decimal place
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.r.c: It is already given that the means are the same. A more exact mean does not tell you the shape of the distribution.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.o.d: The middle value when each class's scores are lined up in order of size
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.r.d: If the mean and the middle value differ, that is a clue that the distribution leans to one side.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.o.e: All the scores in each class (or a table of the number of students in each score range)
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.r.e: This is the most direct information, since it lets you see the distribution itself.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.explain: The mean sums up the scores in a single number and hides how spread out they are and what shape they have. You need the highest and lowest scores, the middle value, and all the scores to know whether the distributions are similar.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.acc.0: You can check the spread and the distribution directly. Adding the middle value lets you see right away whether it leans to one side.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s1.acc.1: The middle value and all the data are enough to check the distribution.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different examples of 5 scores whose mean is 70 points and whose middle score (median) is 80 points or more. Scores are from 0 to 100. Put them into a, b, c, d, e from the smallest score in order.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s2.hint.0: If the mean is 70, what must the sum of the five scores be?
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s2.hint.1: If the middle value is 80 or more, what is the least the middle score and the two higher scores can add up to? How much is left for the other two scores?
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Scores must be at least 0 and at most 100.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s2.ok.c2: You put the scores in order from the smallest.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Put the scores in the order a, b, c, d, e so that each is the same as or bigger than the one before.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The scores add up to 350, so the mean is 70.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s2.fail.c3: For the mean to be 70, the five scores must add up to 350.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s2.ok.c4: The middle score is 80 or more.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s2.fail.c4: The middle (3rd) score must be 80 or more.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s2.explain: For example, 20, 50, 80, 100, 100 has a mean of 70 but a middle value of 80. When a few low scores pull the mean down, the mean and the middle value become different.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s3.prompt: If you describe a class like your example, with a mean of 70 points but a middle value of 80 points or more, only as 'a class with a mean of 70,' what misunderstanding could arise?
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write using the five scores you made yourself.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the picture of the class that a person hearing only the mean would imagine with the real picture.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If you hear only the mean, ...
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation connect to the score example you made?
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say why the idea 'same mean means same class' is risky?
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s3.model.0: If you only say the mean is 70 points, it sounds like most scores are near 70, but in fact more than half could be 80 or above, with one or two low scores pulling the mean down.
x-m-el-sta-03.s.s3.model.1: Looking only at the mean, the two classes look the same, but looking at the score distribution, one class has a lowered mean because of a few low scores, so they are different.

x-m-el-sta-04.title: The real story behind a neighborhood with a 400만 원 average
x-m-el-sta-04.goal: When data is revealed step by step, correct your first interpretation of the mean, and explain how an extreme value affects the mean.
x-m-el-sta-04.material: This is an advertising line for a neighborhood: 'The average monthly income of our 5 residents is 400만 원!' The data is revealed step by step.
x-m-el-sta-04.thinking.0: Revise your interpretation after seeing new data
x-m-el-sta-04.thinking.1: Compare how much the mean and the median react to an extreme value
x-m-el-sta-04.thinking.2: Rewrite it in wording that causes no misunderstanding
x-m-el-sta-04.prereq.0: The meaning of mean (arithmetic mean) and median
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose the most fitting thought.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write separately what the mean tells you and what it does not.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.hint.1: Use the newly revealed data to check, one by one, the guesses you made in the earlier step.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.0.info: Only the advertising line has been revealed: 'The average monthly income of 5 residents is 400만 원.'
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the most reasonable guess from this line alone?
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.0.after: From the mean alone, you cannot tell how similar the residents are or whether the values lean to one side.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Most residents earn around 400만 원 a month
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: A mean of 400 does not mean that most are near 400. One large value can raise the mean.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Residents' incomes probably differ, but we cannot yet tell how spread out they are
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You pointed out that there are things the mean alone cannot tell you.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: There must be at least 3 residents who earn more than 400만 원
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The number of values above the mean is not decided by the mean alone. One large value can also pull the mean up.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: No resident earns less than 400만 원
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Unless everyone's income is exactly 400, there are values smaller than the mean.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.1.info: The data has been revealed. The monthly incomes of the 5 residents are 200, 220, 240, 260, 1080 (만 원). The total is 2000만 원, so the mean of 400만 원 is correct.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Which is the right evaluation of the advertising line?
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.1.after: Four residents earn 200 to 260만 원, but one earns 1080만 원, which raised the mean. Even if the calculation is correct, the line can cause a misunderstanding.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The calculation is wrong. The mean cannot be 400
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: 200+220+240+260+1080=2000 and 2000÷5=400, so the calculation is correct. The problem is not the calculation but the impression that number gives.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The calculation is correct, but it makes 400 read as if it were most residents' income
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You pointed out that even when the mean is right, the reader's guess can differ from the data.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The mean is always more reliable than the median, so the line is the most accurate
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Which representative value is better depends on the shape of the data. In this data, the middle value (240) and the mean are very different.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It is always right to remove 1080 as a strange value and recompute the mean
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: That would erase the value of a resident who really lives there. Rather than removing it, you should also report how much that value affected the mean.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.2.info: The resident who earned 1080만 원 moved away. The incomes of the remaining 4 (200, 220, 240, 260) stay the same. The mean dropped from 400 to 230, while the middle value changed only a little, from 240 to 230 (the middle of 220 and 240).
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: What can you tell from this change?
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.2.after: One extreme value has a large effect on the mean and a small effect on the middle value. When you give a mean, you should also report how spread out the data is.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The mean dropped because the remaining residents' incomes went down
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The incomes of the remaining 4 stayed the same. The mean dropped because the large value left.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: One value can move the mean a lot, and the middle value is shaken less by such a value
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You found that the mean and the median react to an extreme value by different amounts.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The middle value is always a better representative value than the mean
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: In this data the middle value is stable, but which one is better depends on the data and the purpose.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The amount of data went down, so the mean must go down
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: If a small value leaves, the mean can go up. This time a large value left, so it went down.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s1.reflect: How did the impression of the line differ between hearing only the mean and seeing all the data? What would be good to report along with the mean?
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s2.prompt: Rewrite the advertising line 'The average monthly income of 5 residents is 400만 원!' so that it causes no misunderstanding.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s2.hint.0: Add one more number besides the mean.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s2.hint.1: Say with numbers what range 'most' refers to.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: When you read your revised line, can you picture what the residents are really like?
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you reduce the misunderstanding without getting rid of the mean?
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s2.model.0: Of the 5 residents, 4 earn 200 to 260만 원 a month, and one earns 1080만 원, so the mean is 400만 원.
x-m-el-sta-04.s.s2.model.1: The mean is 400만 원, but the middle value is 240만 원.

x-m-el-sta-05.title: Few tosses and many tosses: chance or rigging?
x-m-el-sta-05.goal: Using simulation data, judge the idea behind hypothesis testing: even with the same ratio, how hard it is to explain a result by 'chance' depends on the number of trials.
x-m-el-sta-05.material: Jihoon tossed a coin and said, 'I think this coin was made to land heads more often!' You ran a computer simulation to see how often a result like this happens with a fair coin (a coin where heads and tails are equally likely). Simulation results: (a) Tossing a fair coin 10 times was repeated 1000 times, and 7 or more heads came up in about 170 of them. (b) Tossing a fair coin 100 times was repeated 1000 times, and 70 or more heads never came up even once. Jihoon's actual results are Case A (7 heads in 10 tosses) and Case B (70 heads in 100 tosses).
x-m-el-sta-05.thinking.0: Compare the strength of two pieces of evidence
x-m-el-sta-05.thinking.1: Judge how well chance can explain a result
x-m-el-sta-05.thinking.2: Tell apart being certain and being suspicious
x-m-el-sta-05.prereq.0: The meaning of probability and repeated trials
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s1.prompt: Which is stronger evidence for Jihoon's claim that 'the coin was made to land heads more often'?
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s1.hint.0: Find which of simulations (a) and (b) each of Case A and Case B matches.
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s1.hint.1: Compare, in each simulation, how many times a fair coin also gave that result.
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s1.o.a: Case A. Getting 7 heads in a small number of tosses is the more surprising result
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s1.r.a: In simulation (a), even a fair coin gave 7 or more heads out of 10 in about 170 of 1000 runs. A result that happens often is not surprising.
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s1.o.b: Both cases are 70% heads, so the evidence is equally strong
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s1.r.b: Even if the ratio is the same, a different number of tosses changes how likely it is to happen by chance. Compare simulation tables (a) and (b).
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s1.o.c: Case B. A fair coin did not give a result like this in the simulation
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s1.r.c: You found that the more tosses there are, the harder a result is to explain by chance alone.
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s1.o.d: Neither is evidence. A fair coin can also land heads 70% of the time
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s1.r.d: 'It can happen' and 'it happens often' are different. In (b) it was so rare that it never happened.
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s1.explain: Even with a fair coin, 7 or more heads out of 10 happens fairly often (about 17%), but 70 or more heads out of 100 never happened in the simulation. Even with the same ratio, more tosses make it harder to explain by chance. This is the basic idea of testing a hypothesis.
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s2.prompt: From the result of Case B, can you be 100% sure that 'this coin was made to land heads more often'? Write your judgment and reason.
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s2.hint.0: Show the degree without using the words 'absolutely' and 'not at all.'
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s2.hint.1: Using simulation (b) as evidence, say how rare a result like this is with a fair coin.
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does your judgment say how suspicious it is, rather than 'definitely not' or 'definitely so'?
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you use the simulation result as evidence?
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s2.model.0: We can't be sure. Even a fair coin can very rarely give 70 heads. But it is too rare to call chance, so it is quite likely that the coin was rigged.
x-m-el-sta-05.s.s2.model.1: It's hard to say for sure. The probability that a fair coin gives this result by chance is not 0. But it never happened in the simulation, so it is worth being suspicious.

x-m-el-sta-06.title: Choosing a sample size between a margin of error and a budget
x-m-el-sta-06.goal: Find a sample size that satisfies both the margin-of-error condition and the budget condition, and tell apart problems that a larger sample size does not solve.
x-m-el-sta-06.material: You want to estimate the mean daily smartphone use (in minutes) of students at a school using a sample. The population standard deviation is known to be 20 minutes, and when estimating the population mean with the sample mean, the margin of error (about 95% confidence) is 2×20÷√n minutes (n is the sample size). Surveying one person costs 3000원, and the budget is 360000원.
x-m-el-sta-06.thinking.0: Find several answers that satisfy both conditions at the same time
x-m-el-sta-06.thinking.1: Read the relationship between sample size and margin of error
x-m-el-sta-06.thinking.2: Tell apart problems that size solves and problems it does not
x-m-el-sta-06.prereq.0: The meaning of sample mean, population mean, and margin of error
x-m-el-sta-06.prereq.1: Reading a formula and turning it into an inequality (grade 10 level)
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s1.prompt: Find 3 different sample sizes n that keep the margin of error at 4 minutes or less without exceeding the budget.
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s1.hint.0: First check the margin of error and the cost when n=100.
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how the margin of error and the cost each change as n grows, and find both ends of the range.
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s1.ok.c1: n is an integer that is at least 1.
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s1.fail.c1: The sample size must be an integer that is at least 1.
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s1.ok.c2: The margin of error is 4 minutes or less.
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s1.fail.c2: The margin of error (2×20÷√n) is greater than 4 minutes.
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s1.fail.c3: The survey cost (3000×n) exceeds the budget of 360000원.
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s1.explain: For 40÷√n ≤ 4, you need √n ≥ 10, that is, n ≥ 100, and the budget gives n ≤ 120. So every integer from 100 to 120 works.
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s2.prompt: The surveyor increases the sample size from 100 to 400 and says, 'Now the estimate can't be wrong.' What is the most fitting evaluation?
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s2.hint.0: Put n=100 and n=400 into the formula and compare the margins of error.
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s2.hint.1: Separate what a larger sample size reduces from what it cannot reduce.
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s2.o.a: Right. With 400 people, the sample mean equals the population mean no matter how the sample was chosen
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s2.r.a: Even if the sample gets bigger, the sample mean does not become exactly equal to the population mean. This is even more true if the way of choosing is biased.
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s2.o.b: The margin of error is cut in half, but if the sample was chosen in a biased way, the bias remains
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s2.r.b: You told apart the error that size reduces from the bias that comes from how the sample is chosen.
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s2.o.c: Wrong. Increasing the sample size does not reduce the margin of error at all
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s2.r.c: In the formula, when n gets bigger, 40÷√n gets smaller. Put in n=100 and n=400 yourself and compare.
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s2.o.d: The margin of error becomes one quarter, so the estimate can hardly be wrong
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s2.r.d: When n becomes 4 times as large, √n becomes 2 times as large, so the margin of error is not one quarter. Put in the values yourself and check.
x-m-el-sta-06.s.s2.explain: When n goes from 100 to 400, which is 4 times as large, √n becomes 2 times as large, so the margin of error is cut in half, from 4 minutes to 2 minutes. Even so, bias that comes from how the sample was chosen does not disappear when you increase the size.

x-m-el-sta-07.title: If we sleep more, will scores go up?
x-m-el-sta-07.goal: Tell apart what correlation data does and does not say, and design the kind of study needed to check causation.
x-m-el-sta-07.material: A survey recorded 200 students' average daily sleep time and their math test scores. When the points are plotted on a plane, the points spread toward the upper right, meaning scores are generally higher for longer sleep time. The correlation coefficient is about 0.6. The students lived as usual, and no one was made to change their sleep time.
x-m-el-sta-07.thinking.0: Pick out the claims the data supports
x-m-el-sta-07.thinking.2: Design a study to check causation
x-m-el-sta-07.prereq.0: The meaning of scatter plot and correlation coefficient (positive correlation, negative correlation)
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything that can be said from this survey data alone.
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s1.hint.0: Tell apart whether each sentence says 'they change together' or 'changing one changes the other.'
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s1.hint.1: Reread who decided the sleep time in the survey.
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s1.o.a: If you increase sleep time, anyone's score goes up
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s1.r.a: 'Anyone' applies a tendency to every individual. This survey is not an experiment where sleep time was changed.
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s1.o.b: Students with longer sleep time tend to have higher scores
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s1.r.b: You read the meaning of correlation, a tendency to change together, correctly.
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s1.o.c: When scores go up, students come to sleep better
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s1.r.c: Interpreting the direction the other way around also cannot be confirmed from this data alone.
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s1.o.d: There may be students in this data who sleep long but have low scores
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s1.r.d: You realized that the tendency does not show up in every student in the same way.
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s1.o.e: This data shows that there is no relationship between sleep time and scores
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s1.r.e: A correlation coefficient of 0.6 is far from no relationship (near 0).
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s1.explain: Correlation only tells you a tendency to change together, not what the cause is. And since it is a tendency, there are students who are exceptions.
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s2.prompt: How should a study be designed to find out whether increasing sleep time raises scores (whether it is the cause)? Write one or two sentences.
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s2.hint.0: Think about who could decide the sleep time, instead of letting students decide it.
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s2.hint.1: Think about how to split the two groups to be compared so it is fair.
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you make sure other factors besides sleep time that affect scores are spread similarly across the two groups?
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is your design free of harm to the students?
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s2.model.0: Randomly split the students into two groups, have only one group sleep longer for 2 weeks, and compare the change in test scores of the two groups.
x-m-el-sta-07.s.s2.model.1: Divide similar students by lottery, have only one side go to bed early with all other conditions the same, and then compare scores.

x-m-el-sta-08.title: Do more firefighters mean more damage?
x-m-el-sta-08.goal: Find the line in a report that jumps from correlation to causation, and rewrite it within what the data can say.
x-m-el-sta-08.material: This is part of a city's fire report.
x-m-el-sta-08.thinking.2: Rewrite as a sentence the data supports
x-m-el-sta-08.prereq.0: The meaning of correlation (a tendency to change together)
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line that the data does not support.
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s1.hint.0: Sort each line into whether it says 'they change together' or 'it is the cause.'
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether another factor could make both the number of firefighters and the damage amount grow.
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s1.line.0: For each fire, we recorded the number of firefighters sent and the damage amount caused by the fire.
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s1.line.1: The more firefighters were sent to a fire, the larger the damage amount tended to be.
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s1.line.2: So there is a positive correlation between the number of firefighters and the damage amount.
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s1.line.3: Therefore the firefighters sent are the cause of the larger damage amount.
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s1.line.4: To reduce damage, we should reduce the number of firefighters sent in the future.
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s1.explain: Line 4 turned a tendency to grow together (correlation) into a cause, that firefighters make the damage bigger. It may be because when a big fire breaks out, more firefighters are sent and the damage is larger too. Line 5 is a policy suggestion based on this wrong cause, so it also has no basis. Lines 1 to 3 are sentences within what the data tells us.
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s2.prompt: Rewrite line 4 ('Therefore the firefighters sent are the cause of the larger damage amount.') as a sentence the data can support, and write why you changed it that way.
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s2.hint.0: Imagine how the number of firefighters sent differs between a big fire and a small fire.
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s2.hint.1: Find words you can use instead of 'is the cause.'
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s2.placeholder: e.g. The number of firefighters and the damage amount ...
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does your revised sentence avoid claiming a cause?
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check that the other factor you gave could affect both the number of firefighters and the damage amount?
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s2.model.0: The number of firefighters and the damage amount tend to grow together. A bigger fire may mean more firefighters were sent and more damage was done, so we cannot call it the cause.
x-m-el-sta-08.s.s2.model.1: Another factor, the size of the fire, may have made both values bigger, so with this data we can only say there is a correlation.

x-m-el-sta-09.title: Making a graph that fools with bar heights
x-m-el-sta-09.goal: By making one yourself, see that starting the vertical axis at a value other than 0 changes how the ratio of bar heights looks, and choose the conditions for an honest graph.
x-m-el-sta-09.material: Monthly sales of two products are almost the same: 52 for A and 56 for B. When drawing this data as a bar graph, you can start the vertical axis at some number s other than 0 (cutting off everything below it). Then the visible bar heights become 52−s for A and 56−s for B. (If s=0, the visible heights are 52 and 56.)
x-m-el-sta-09.thinking.0: Check how the axis setting affects visual comparison
x-m-el-sta-09.thinking.1: Find several values that satisfy a condition
x-m-el-sta-09.thinking.2: Pick out honest ways to present data
x-m-el-sta-09.prereq.1: The meaning of a ratio (how many times)
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s1.prompt: Find 3 different values of s that make bar B look at least 3 times as tall as bar A. (s is at least 0 and less than 52.)
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s1.hint.0: Put in s=0, 40, 48 and find the ratio of the visible heights for each.
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s1.hint.1: Find roughly the value of s where the ratio starts to be 3 or more.
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s1.var.s: Starting value of the vertical axis
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s1.ok.c1: s is at least 0 and less than 52.
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s1.fail.c1: s must be at least 0 and less than 52.
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s1.ok.c2: Bar B looks at least 3 times as tall as bar A.
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s1.fail.c2: B's visible height (56−s) is less than 3 times A's visible height (52−s).
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s1.explain: If s=50, the visible heights are 2 for A and 6 for B, so exactly 3 times. If s is greater than 50 and less than 52, the ratio gets even larger. The actual sales are 52 and 56, only about 1.08 times, yet the graph makes them look very different.
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.prompt: How should you fix a misleading graph like this to make it honest? Choose everything that fits.
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.hint.0: Tell apart whether each method helps the reader understand the values correctly or steers the impression to one side.
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.hint.1: For bar heights to be proportional to the values, where must the vertical axis start?
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.o.a: Draw the vertical axis of the bar graph starting from 0
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.r.a: You chose the most basic way to make bar heights proportional to the values.
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.o.b: Color only bar B in a dark color so it stands out
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.r.b: Emphasizing one side with color distorts the impression even more. The first question is whether the heights honestly show the values.
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.o.c: Make the scale marks closer together to make the difference between the two bars look bigger
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.r.c: Adjusting the scale spacing to enlarge the difference is just one more way of misleading.
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.o.d: Write the actual values, such as 52 and 56, above the bars
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.r.d: You let the reader check the values directly instead of the heights.
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.o.e: When cutting the vertical axis, draw an axis-break mark and let the reader know
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.r.e: You chose a method that does not hide the fact that the axis was cut.
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.explain: In a bar graph, the height must be proportional to the value. Start the axis at 0, or if you cut it, mark that fact and write the actual values so the reader is not fooled. Enlarging the difference with color or scale spacing is actually distortion.
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.acc.0: Starting the axis at 0 and writing the values is honest enough. It would be even better to also know how to mark a cut axis.
x-m-el-sta-09.s.s2.acc.1: Even if you cut the axis, marking it and writing the values keeps readers from being fooled. If possible, starting at 0 is simpler.

x-m-el-sta-10.title: Drawing multiple-answer data as a pie chart
x-m-el-sta-10.goal: Find why the percentages of multiple-answer data cannot be shown in a pie chart, and choose a suitable graph.
x-m-el-sta-10.material: At one school, all 100 students were asked, 'Choose all the sports you like (you may choose more than one),' and a report was written.
x-m-el-sta-10.thinking.0: Judge whether the kind of graph fits the nature of the data
x-m-el-sta-10.thinking.1: Explain why the total goes over 100%
x-m-el-sta-10.thinking.2: Fix it with a suitable graph
x-m-el-sta-10.prereq.0: The meaning of pie chart and ratio
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one wrong line in the report.
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s1.hint.0: Find what you get when you add all four percentages.
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s1.hint.1: Recall that the sectors of a pie chart divide the whole without overlapping.
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s1.line.0: 60 students chose soccer, 45 chose basketball, 30 chose volleyball, and 25 chose jump rope.
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s1.line.1: The percentage of students who chose each sport is soccer 60%, basketball 45%, volleyball 30%, and jump rope 25%.
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s1.line.2: If these percentages are shown in a pie chart, the central angles of the four sectors are 216 degrees, 162 degrees, 108 degrees, and 90 degrees.
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s1.line.3: If you put all four sectors together, they make one complete circle.
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s1.line.4: So we can say that 60% of all students chose soccer.
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s1.explain: Lines 3 and 4 are the problem. Because multiple choices were allowed, one student chose several sports, so the percentages add up to 160%, and the central angles add up to 576 degrees, more than one full turn of the circle (360 degrees). Line 5 is correct, because 60 of the 100 students chose soccer.
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s2.prompt: What is the most suitable graph to honestly show this data?
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s2.hint.0: Tell apart whether the items in the graph are parts that don't overlap or separate values.
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether each item's percentage has the same denominator of 100 students.
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s2.o.a: Divide the percentages by 160 so they add to 100%, draw a pie chart, and leave the title as it is
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s2.r.a: If you change the values, they become 'percent of responses' instead of 'percent of students,' which doesn't match the title.
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s2.o.b: Leave the pie chart as it is and write 'total 160%' in small print below
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s2.r.b: This only adds an explanation to a graph that breaks the rule that the full circle is the whole.
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s2.o.c: Change the pie chart to a bar graph and show, on each bar, the percentage of students who chose that sport
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s2.r.c: You chose a kind of graph that can show each sport as an independent item.
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s2.o.d: Split into soccer and 'the rest,' draw a pie chart with two sectors, and use 45+30+25 for the rest
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s2.r.d: Adding up the rest gives 100%, which differs from the 40% of students who did not choose soccer. The double-counted values are still there.
x-m-el-sta-10.s.s2.explain: In multiple-answer data, one student falls into several items, so the percentages can add to more than 100%. In this case, showing each item separately with its own bar fits the nature of the data.
